doc.title: Marty Grosz interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 4, 1995

title: Learning to read stock arrangements and chord symbols
summary: He found stock arrangements like Stomping at the Savoy baffling, and notes guitar parts were mostly rhythm.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: Yes. Except there was a difference I think. We knew, it didn’t take long before you knew that a lot of hard work was ahead of you before you even could knock on the door, I think. Because although we fantasized and posed in front of the mirror with our instruments, guys with their clarinets and trumpets and everything like that, when you actually went to see one of these bands, you had some youthful arrogance, well I’ll get there, but it soon became apparent that it wasn’t all that easy. You know first of all in those days, all — not all bands — but most of the bands read. You had to read. And most of the dance orchestrations, I mean that’s what most music was for, starting off with high school dances, and then you know into theaters and stuff, and all these guys had their nose in the paper. And the first time I remember looking at one of those stock arrangements of “Stomping at the Savoy,” I thought well this is, you know, hieroglyphics. You need the rosetta stone to decipher this. What in the hell is a D flat ninth? What is that? And what is a G flat minor sixth? And all that stuff.
They had the slashes and the chords?
Yeah, yeah. The guitar parts were mostly rhythm parts in those days you know.
